name: UHFKill
price_note: US$1,650 direct from NFCKill (listed sold out on nfckill.com at check time). Lab401 stocks it at EUR1,495 (~US$1,738 at the EUR/USD rate on price_checked date), made-to-order, ~5 day dispatch. An 'Embedded' variant for micro-tags baked into eyewear/plastic goods is EUR1,950 (~US$2,267) at Lab401. First-pass figure of $1,750 is close to the Lab401-converted price.
skill_note: Point, hold 5cm from the tag for the pulse duration, done - no protocol knowledge needed. The judgment call is knowing which tags in a shipment are UHF vs the HF/LF tags a standard NFC Kill handles.
build_note: Ships as a complete mains-powered unit; no assembly. It is not a device you flash or configure.
summary: A mains-powered electromagnetic-pulse emitter that permanently disables passive UHF RFID tags (800-960MHz, EPC Gen1/Gen2) used for retail inventory and supply-chain tracking, at up to 5cm range. It is the UHF sibling of the same company's HF/LF 'NFC Kill' deactivator, built for the specific case - apparel, footwear, eyewear - where a UHF tag is sewn or moulded in and cannot be cut out.
honest_take: This is a bench tool, not a pocket gadget: 2.5kg, mains-powered at up to 15kW instantaneous pulse power, and it needs to sit within 5cm of the tag. It does not 'jam' or block UHF reads - it physically burns out the tag's antenna-to-chip bond with an induced pulse, which is irreversible and detectable (the tag is dead, not hidden). NFCKill's own claim is ~98% coverage of common antenna geometries, not 100%, so a rack of unusual tags may need the reader/verification step (Lab401 pairs it with the Industrial Handheld UHF Reader for exactly this). The obvious misconception is that this is a covert shoplifting tool - it is loud, requires a power outlet, and is marketed and priced for legitimate supply-chain/loss-prevention/returns-processing workflows, not something you carry into a store. It also does nothing at all to HF/LF tags - that is a different product from the same maker.
best_for: Retailers and returns-processing centres deactivating UHF EAS tags before resale or recycling
Verifying UHF EAS/anti-theft tag designs during product development
Security researchers auditing UHF RFID supply-chain deployments
not_for: Covert or portable use - it is a 2.5kg mains-powered bench unit, not concealable
HF/LF tags (access badges, most payment cards) - use the standard NFC Kill instead
Guaranteed 100% tag coverage - some antenna geometries are missed

hf_1356_emulate.note: Not a reader/emulator of any kind.

uhf_rfid_write.note: No write capability either - destruction is the entire function; there is no protocol stack here to write EPC memory banks with.

legal.notes: Deactivating UHF tags on goods you own or are authorised to process (returns, recycling, retail operations, research) is not itself restricted in most jurisdictions - this is a supply-chain tool sold openly to retailers. It becomes a legal problem the same way any tool does when used to facilitate theft (defeating an anti-theft device on merchandise that is not yours to deactivate). Check local retail-loss-prevention and consumer-protection law if deploying commercially.

name: Long-range iCLASS RFID Capture System
firmware_note: Runs a variant of PPE's Doppelganger_Core ESP32-S3 firmware (the same firmware family as the standalone 'Doppelganger Core' dev board already in this database), pre-flashed and pre-wired inside a commercial reader shell. It decodes Wiegand output from the host reader and pushes captured credentials to the phone-based 'Doppelganger Assistant' UI; deeper card-format coverage (MIFARE, Corporate 1000, etc.) sits behind paid firmware tiers exactly as it does on the bare Core board.
price_note: US$845 direct from PPE's own store (store.physicalexploit.com), the manufacturer. Lab401 resells the same unit at EUR895 (~US$1,041 at the EUR/USD rate on price_checked date) plus a EUR-priced power supply add-on. First-pass figure of $895 appears to have taken the Lab401 euro price as if it were dollars.
skill_note: Operating the reader-in-a-bag is trivial via the phone app; getting useful results requires understanding iCLASS's legacy/SE/SEOS split and knowing the target site's configuration well enough to plan a brush-by.
build_note: Ships fully built: a genuine HID iCLASS R90SE industrial reader with the Doppelgänger Core module pre-installed and wired to its Wiegand output, in a protective case meant for bag carry.
summary: A genuine HID iCLASS R90SE industrial-grade reader with a Doppelgänger Core capture module wired into its Wiegand line, built to be carried in a bag or backpack and read iCLASS badges off people's belts or bags from up to ~45cm. It is the productised, ready-to-carry version of the same Doppelgänger Core hardware already tracked in this database as a bare implant board - here bolted to real long-range reader hardware and cased for field use.
honest_take: The read range comes entirely from the HID R90SE being genuine long-range industrial reader hardware, not from any trick in the Doppelgänger firmware - you could build the same thing yourself for less by buying an R90SE and a bare Doppelgänger Core board (~$60) and wiring them together, which is exactly what this product is. What it captures for iCLASS SE/SEOS cards is the card's identity/CSN, not a working key - PPE's own downgrade-attack language and the wider iCLASS research (including this database's Proxmark3 entry) both note there is no card-only attack on properly configured SE/SEOS; a captured SEOS card only clones cleanly if the site's readers still accept legacy/downgraded credentials. On plain iCLASS Legacy or HID Prox it works exactly as advertised.
best_for: Physical red-team engagements auditing whether staff badges can be brushed in a corridor or lobby
Sites confirmed or suspected to run iCLASS Legacy or downgrade-vulnerable SE/SEOS
Teams who want a turnkey long-range capture rig without building one from a bare Doppelgänger board
not_for: Properly configured iCLASS SEOS deployments with legacy mode disabled - there is no card-only key-recovery attack for that
Anyone without written engagement authorisation - a bag-carried covert credential skimmer is squarely in unauthorised-interception territory otherwise
MIFARE Classic/DESFire key recovery - the reader front end captures UID/identity data only, it does not run cryptanalytic attacks

honest_take: 125kHz HID Prox, Indala, AWID and the other formats this reads are unauthenticated by design - the card broadcasts its ID to anything that energises it, and that has been true since these formats existed. name: Stealth Decoy Reader (SDR v2)
firmware_note: Runs a variant of PPE's Doppelganger_Core ESP32-S3 firmware (the same firmware family as the standalone 'Doppelganger Core' dev board already in this database), pre-flashed and pre-wired inside a commercial reader shell. It decodes Wiegand output from the host reader and pushes captured credentials to the phone-based 'Doppelganger Assistant' UI; deeper card-format coverage (MIFARE, Corporate 1000, etc.) sits behind paid firmware tiers exactly as it does on the bare Core board.
price_note: US$375 direct from PPE's store for the 'Stealth Decoy Reader (SDR) v2' with a genuine reader housing (one of three variants: HID multiCLASS SE RP40, HID Signo 20TKS, or Paxton P75). PPE also sells the bare Doppelganger board alone for $60. Lab401 lists the same product line under two separate SKUs that this record merges: a generic 'Stealth Decoy Reader' spanning EUR125 (module only) to EUR685 (full reader), and a 'Dual Mode Paxton Long Range / Stealth Decoy Reader' at a flat EUR475 (~US$552) which is simply the Paxton P75 configuration of this same product sold as its own listing. Treat any Lab401 price between EUR125 and EUR685 as a configuration of this one item.
skill_note: Installing a convincing decoy at a real door and not getting caught is the actual skill; operating the capture app once it is placed is trivial.
build_note: Ships as a genuine commercial reader (HID multiCLASS SE RP40, HID Signo 20TKS, or Paxton P75, selectable) with the Doppelgänger module pre-installed inside, or as the bare module for building your own housing. Mounts with the included magnetic plate and adhesive strips.
summary: A genuine commercial access-control reader - HID multiCLASS SE, HID Signo, or a Paxton Net2-specific model - with a Doppelgänger Core credential-capture module hidden inside, meant to be mounted beside or in place of a real reader so anyone who badges it hands over their credential. It is the 'looks completely legitimate' counterpart to the bag-carried long-range capture units in the same PPE product line, and the Paxton-specific configuration that some resellers list separately as the 'Dual Mode Paxton Long Range / Stealth Decoy Reader' is the same base product.
honest_take: This device only works because it looks exactly like the reader already on the wall - the entire attack is social engineering plus physical access, not a technical exploit. It supports a long protocol list (iCLASS SE/SEOS/SR, MIFARE Classic/DESFire EV1, HID Prox, AWID, EM4102, T5577, Indala on Signo readers, Paxton Net2), but as with every other device in this batch, supporting a protocol in the Wiegand-tap sense means capturing whatever the real reader already decoded - it does not defeat DESFire or SEOS cryptography, it just sits downstream of a reader that already did the legitimate authentication and taps the wire carrying the result. The 4+ hour battery figure is for the module alone; a full engagement mounting it near an entrance for days needs mains power or repeat battery swaps, neither of which the covert framing advertises. This is, bluntly, a physical-access wiretap wearing a badge reader's clothes.

summary: An open-source 13.56MHz NFC shield built around ST25R3916 - the same NFC chipset used in the Proxmark3 RDV4.01 and other reference platforms - that plugs onto a HydraBus v1 multi-tool board. It reads/writes/emulates ISO14443A, ISO14443B, FeliCa and ISO15693, and includes a genuine real-time RF sniffer mode with a dedicated PulseView decoder, at claimed 12cm+ (ISO14443A) and 16cm+ (ISO15693) ranges.
honest_take: This is not a Flipper-style all-in-one - it is a bare shield that does nothing without a separate HydraBus v1 host, and the whole stack is console-driven with no app. Where it earns its place next to a Proxmark3 is the same ST25R3916 chipset giving genuinely comparable RF performance at a fraction of the price, plus a real hardware sniffer mode most cheap NFC tools lack entirely. What it does not have is a Proxmark3's library of ready-made MIFARE Classic key-recovery attacks (darkside/nested/hardnested) - the firmware gives you raw frame access and expects you to build that yourself. The catch is availability: the official storefront was effectively non-functional when checked (empty shop listing, 404 product page), so budget for the possibility this is easier to find via Digi-Key or an EU reseller than direct from the maker.

summary: A large-antenna variant of D-Logic's PN533-based DL533N reader/writer, trading a normal-size card-reader footprint for an oversized 178x178mm built-in antenna that extends read/write range to about 18cm - enough to sit under a desk or inside a bag rather than needing the card presented directly to it. At 18cm it is meaningfully better than a standard USB reader for a 'reader under a desk/bag' scenario, but it is nowhere near the 40-120cm a tuned Proxmark3 HF antenna or the 45-60cm the PPE long-range capture systems in this same batch claim - PN533 is a fixed-function reader IC, not the reconfigurable RF frontend a Proxmark's FPGA gives you. name: RFID HF Extender Pro
price_note: US$65 direct at Hacker Warehouse, matching the first-pass figure exactly.
skill_note: No electronics knowledge required - it is two coils and a cable, placed by hand.
build_note: Fully passive; no firmware, no configuration, nothing to flash or pair.
summary: Two coupled 13.56MHz HF/NFC antennas - one 60mm, one 27mm - joined by a 30cm IPEX cable. Placed one coil against a reader and the other where you actually want the card presented, the pair passively relays the reader's field (and the card's response) across the cable, physically repositioning where a badge needs to be tapped without moving the reader itself.
honest_take: This sits right on the line the brief for this database explicitly excludes ('plain cables and antennas') - and functionally, that is almost exactly what it is: two passive coils and a cable, with no active circuitry, amplification or protocol handling anywhere in it. It works by simple magnetic coupling, not by decoding and re-transmitting a signal, so it is not a true active NFC relay attack tool (compare to a genuine two-device relay built from two SDRs or NFC readers with a network link between them, which can span arbitrary distances) - it only repositions a reader's existing field by the length of its 30cm cable. The single legitimate niche it fills is exactly what the vendor's own copy admits: freeing a reader from an awkward fixed mounting position during a physical test, not extending range or enabling a long-distance relay attack.
best_for: Repositioning where a badge needs to be presented when a reader is mounted somewhere physically inconvenient to test from
Short-range (cable-length) covert placement during an authorised physical assessment
not_for: Long-distance relay attacks - it is a passive coupler, not an active repeater; range is the 30cm cable length, not metres
Amplifying or extending actual read range beyond a normal reader's native field - it relays the field, it does not boost it
Any protocol-level interaction - it is transparent to whatever the reader and card are already doing
